f:topgunmaverick: Held back two years for the pandemic, then credited with pulling audiences back to cinemas; the cast trained for months to sit in real jets.
f:topsyturvy: Gilbert and Sullivan make The Mikado; its director’s usual improvised method applied to Victorian theatre.
f:torasan1: The first of 48 films with the same wandering pedlar and the same star, a record series.
f:torment: Written by a young man who would soon become the most famous director in Sweden; he also directed its final scene.
f:totalrecall: A Philip K. Dick story about implanted memories, shot in Mexico City with some of the last great practical effects.
f:totoro: Released as a double bill with a war-orphan drama from the same studio. Its forest spirit became the studio’s logo.
f:touchevil: Opens with a three-minute unbroken crane shot and a ticking bomb. The studio recut it; its director wrote a 58-page memo in protest, followed for a 1998 restoration.
f:touchzen: A bamboo-forest fight shot over weeks; the first Chinese-language film honoured at Cannes.
f:toukibouki: A cowherd and a student dream of Paris on a motorbike with cattle horns; restored by Martin Scorsese’s foundation.
f:tousles: A film about two viol players that sent a baroque soundtrack to the top of the French charts.
f:toweringinferno: Two studios had bought rival skyscraper-fire novels, so they merged the projects.
f:toystory: The first feature made entirely by computer; the studio nearly shut it down after a sour early version.
f:toystory2: Planned for video only; almost deleted by an errant command and rescued from a technical director’s home backup.
f:toystory3: The first animated film to gross a billion dollars; the incinerator scene left adults in tears.
f:toystory5: The toys meet their rival: a tablet computer.
f:tradingplaces: Its orange-juice futures finale inspired a real 2010 US trading rule nicknamed after it.
f:traffic: A sensational exposé of forced prostitution that reportedly cost under $6,000 and made a fortune.
f:traffic00: Its director shot it himself under a pseudonym, colour-coding each storyline.
f:train: The story that audiences fled in panic is probably a legend, but the image of the approaching engine is not.
f:trainspotting: Made for £1.7 million in a disused cigarette factory in Glasgow.
f:tramp: The first film to end with the Tramp walking away down a road.
f:treeoflife: A 1950s Texas childhood set against the birth of the universe; the dinosaurs came out of retirement for it, with Douglas Trumbull.
f:treewoodenclogs: Lombard peasants in the 1890s, played by real farmers in their own dialect.
f:trenquelauquen: A botanist vanishes in a small pampas town; a four-hour mystery in two parts that keeps opening onto new ones, made by a collective over several years.
f:triangleofsadness: Models and oligarchs on a luxury yacht, then shipwrecked, where the cleaning lady takes charge. Its director’s second Palme.
f:tribejudah: The first Nollywood film to take more than a billion naira at home.
f:triumphwill: A Nazi rally turned into propaganda spectacle. Studied for its technique and condemned for what it served.
f:truegrit: Its star finally won his Academy prize, playing a one-eyed drunk marshal.
f:truelies: Borrowed Harrier jets from the Marine Corps at $2,000 an hour.
f:trumanshow: Shot in a real Florida planned town called Seaside; its writer’s original script was darker and set in New York.
f:tsotsi: A Johannesburg film, the first African-language winner of the Oscar.
f:turinhorse: Its director said it would be his last film, and it was.
f:turkishstarwars: Lifted its space battles straight from a famous American blockbuster’s footage, without permission.
f:turningred: Sent straight to streaming during the pandemic, to the frustration of its makers.
f:twelveangry: One room, twelve jurors, one holdout. A disappointment in cinemas; a fixture in law schools since.
f:twelvetwelve: The 1979 military coup inside Seoul over one night; young audiences posted their heart rates after watching it.
f:twentydays: Footage shot by the last international journalists inside the besieged city.
f:twentyeightyears: Shot largely on iPhones strapped together in rigs of up to twenty.
f:twilight: Made for $37 million by a mini-major on its first production; its director was replaced for the sequels.
f:twister: The first feature released on DVD in the United States.
f:twostagesisters: Condemned during the Cultural Revolution; its director was persecuted.
f:twotowers: Its digital creature was performed on set by an actor in a motion-capture suit, which changed acting for effects films.
f:ugetsu: A ghost story in mist, with one of the most famous final camera movements in film.
f:umbertod: A pensioner and his dog; its director called it his favourite.
f:umbrellas: Every line is sung, even the ordinary ones; a love story wrecked by the Algerian war, in candy colours.
f:umraojaan: A 19th-century Lucknow courtesan-poet; its ghazals are still sung.
f:umut: A cab driver sells everything to dig for treasure. Seized by censors, it was smuggled out to Cannes.
f:unagi: Won its director his second Palme.
f:uncutgems: Two hours of a Diamond District jeweller making one bad bet after another; the brothers spent ten years getting it made.
f:underground28: A love triangle on the London Underground. Not the 1995 film on your list, but a nice rhyme.
f:underground95: People live in a cellar for twenty years believing the war never ended; its director quit film for a time over accusations it was propaganda.
f:underskin: Glasgow men who got into a van with a movie star were filmed by hidden cameras and told only afterwards.
f:undersunsatan: Booed at the prize-giving; its director raised a fist: "If you don’t like me, I can tell you I don’t like you either."
f:underworld: An early gangster film that helped set the genre’s rules.
f:unforgiven: Its director held the script for a decade until he was old enough to play the lead.
f:unknown: A circus knife-thrower pretends to have no arms, then makes that pretence permanent.
f:untouchables: Its station-steps shootout borrows a pram from a 1925 Soviet film.
f:up09: Its four-minute wordless marriage montage opened Cannes.
f:upkar: Made at a prime minister’s suggestion to celebrate soldiers and farmers.
f:uridhallan75: Credited with changing Egypt's divorce law.
f:usher: A future master of surrealism worked on it as assistant director.
f:utu: A Māori scout turns against the colonial army in the 1870s.
f:vagabond: A young drifter found frozen in a ditch, reconstructed through the people she met.
f:valleydolls: Savaged by critics and loved as camp ever since.
f:vamonosvilla: An unsentimental revolution film that flopped for its studio, then was hailed as one of Mexico’s best.
f:vampires: A ten-part serial about a gang of Paris criminals; its catsuited villainess took her name from an anagram.
f:vampyr: Shot through gauze for a hazy, half-dreamt look, with mostly non-professional actors.
f:variety: The camera swings with the trapeze artists.
f:verdoux: A dark comedy about a wife-killer, boycotted amid attacks on its maker’s politics.
f:verdugo: An undertaker inherits his father-in-law’s job as executioner; a satire the Franco regime tried to suppress.
f:vermiglio: A mountain village in the Italian Alps in the last winter of the Second World War; the teacher’s daughters, a Sicilian deserter, and a marriage. Spoken in the local dialect.
f:veronikavoss: Its director died months after its premiere, aged 37, with over forty films made.
f:vertigo: A mixed reception in 1958; in 2012 critics voted it the greatest film ever made.
f:victim: A barrister risks his career to expose a gang blackmailing gay men. The first English-language film to say the word “homosexual”, and credited with helping change the law.
f:vidassecas: A family fleeing drought across the Brazilian backlands, shot in blinding light.
f:videodrome: "Long live the new flesh." A Toronto cable boss finds a signal that grows tumours.
f:vigil: The first New Zealand film in competition at Cannes.
f:virginiawoolf: Its profanity helped break the old production code; a debut for its director.
f:viridiana: Its director was invited back to Spain after decades in exile; the film won the Riviera and was promptly banned by Franco, and the Vatican condemned it.
f:vivafreedom: The first Korean film made after liberation from Japanese rule.
f:volgavolga38: Said to be Stalin's favourite film; he sent a copy to Roosevelt.
f:wadjda: The first feature shot entirely in Saudi Arabia, by its first woman director, who directed street scenes from inside a van.
f:wagesfear: Four desperate men drive trucks of nitroglycerine over mountain roads.
f:wagthedog: A fake war to distract from a presidential sex scandal; a real one broke a month after release.
f:wakandaforever: Rewritten after the death of its star into a film about grief.
f:wakeinfright: A teacher stranded in an outback town of beer and kangaroo hunts. Lost for decades; its negative was found in a Pittsburgh bin marked for destruction.
f:wallstreet: "Greed, for lack of a better word, is good." Traders took it as a recruiting film.
f:warpeace56: An Italian-American version whose success provoked the Soviet Union to make its own, the one on your list.
f:warpeace66: Released in four parts over two years, running about seven hours. With the Red Army supplying extras and museums lending props, it was among the most expensive films ever made.
f:waterfront: A former boxer who “coulda been a contender”; many read it as its director’s defence of naming names to Congress.
f:waterloo70: Fifteen thousand Soviet soldiers stood in as the two armies; the film lost a fortune.
f:waterworld: The most expensive film ever made at the time; its floating atoll set sank in a storm.
f:wavelength: A 45-minute zoom across a loft toward a photograph on the wall.
f:waydowneast: Its lead lay on real ice floes for the climax, her hand trailing in the freezing river.
f:waynesworld: Revived a Queen song from 1975 into the American Top 5.
f:wayofdragon: Ends with a duel against an American karate champion in the Roman Colosseum.
f:wayofwater: Thirteen years after the first film; the actors learned to hold their breath for underwater motion capture.
f:weapons: Seventeen children from one class run out of their houses at 2:17 a.m.; its script started a bidding war.
f:weddingbanquet: The most profitable film of its year by ratio of cost to gross.
f:weekend: Its eight-minute traffic jam ends with the words “end of cinema”.
f:weirdmob: An Italian migrant in Sydney; made by an exiled British director and a big Australian hit.
f:welcomemarshall: A Castilian village dresses up as Andalusia to impress passing American aid officials, who drive straight through.
f:wenttheday: An English village occupied by disguised German soldiers; startlingly violent for its time.
f:westindies: Three centuries of slavery and migration as a musical, staged inside one enormous slave ship built in a disused Paris factory.
f:westsidestory: Won ten Academy prizes; its co-director was fired during the shoot for going over budget.
f:whalehunting: A road comedy that was the biggest Korean hit of its year.
f:whatsupdoc: A screwball comedy in the 1930s mould, with four identical plaid overnight bags.
f:wherefriendhouse: A boy crosses the hills to return a classmate’s notebook before he gets expelled; its zig-zag path became an emblem of Iranian cinema.
f:whichweserve: The story of a destroyer told through its crew’s memories; the co-director’s first credit.
f:whiplash: Shot in nineteen days; its drummer really bled.
f:whiskygalore: Islanders salvage the cargo of a wrecked whisky ship, based on a real wartime wreck.
f:whitechristmas: The top film of 1954, and the first in a new sharper widescreen process.
f:whitegold: A Cantonese opera film and a huge hit that established Cantonese-language sound cinema.
f:whiterose: Its singer-star’s songs made it one of the first big Arabic musical hits.
f:whitesun: A Red Army soldier escorts a harem across Central Asia; cosmonauts watch it before every launch.
f:whoopee: The top film of 1930, with early overhead dance numbers.
f:wicked: Its makers planted nine million real tulips for the Munchkinland set.
f:wickerman: Cut down and dumped as a B-picture; its villain called it his best film and promoted it for free.
f:wifebelikearose35: One of the first Japanese films released commercially in America.
f:wildatheart: Won the top prize at Cannes to boos; its lead wears a snakeskin jacket as a symbol of individuality.
f:wildbunch: Aging outlaws on the Mexican border; its slow-motion bloodbaths shocked 1969 audiences.
f:wildparty: Its director is credited with rigging an early boom microphone so her star could move while talking.
f:wildrobot: Drawn to look painted, a new style for its studio.
f:wildstrawberries: The last role of the great silent director from the 1920s.
f:wind: The studio imposed a happier ending.
f:windrises: A fictionalised life of the designer of the Zero fighter; announced as its director’s retirement film.
f:wings: The first winner of the top Academy prize, with real aerial combat photography.
f:wingsofdesire: Angels listen to Berliners’ thoughts, filmed two years before the Wall came down; an American TV detective plays himself, a former angel.
f:winnetou: A German western from a 19th-century adventure novelist; a bigger hit in West Germany than any Hollywood film that year.
f:wintersbone: Shot in the Missouri Ozarks with locals in half the parts; made its nineteen-year-old lead a star.
f:witch15: Its seventeenth-century dialogue was taken from diaries and court records of the time.
f:withinourgates: The oldest surviving film by an African American director, a direct answer to the racism of a 1915 epic.
f:withnail: Two out-of-work actors in 1969 Camden flee to a Lake District cottage; its teetotal lead had never been drunk before playing a legendary drunk.
f:wizardofoz: Lost money at first; yearly television broadcasts from 1956 made it perhaps the most-watched film ever.
f:wolfwarrior2: For years the biggest Chinese film ever at home.
f:womanmoon: Invented the rocket-launch countdown, for dramatic effect.
f:womanparis: A drama its director barely appears in. It flopped but influenced a generation of sophisticated comedy.
f:womeninlove: Famous for a nude firelit wrestling match.
f:womenverge: Gazpacho spiked with sleeping pills; its director’s international breakthrough.
f:womenwomen20c: A Santa Barbara single mother in 1979 enlists two younger women to help raise her son.
f:wonderfullife: Lost money and helped sink its new company. A lapsed copyright put it on television every Christmas, and it became a fixture.
f:wonderwoman: The No Man’s Land sequence was the one scene the studio wanted cut.
f:wongfeihung: The first of a long-running series about a real Cantonese martial artist and healer.
f:woodstock: Three days of mud and music; a young Martin Scorsese was among its editors.
f:workers: Part of the first paid public film show, held in a Paris café basement in December 1895.
f:wuthering39: Filmed on California hills dressed with imported heather; its lead and director clashed throughout.
f:wutheringheights: The quotation marks are part of the title, signalling a loose version of the novel.
f:wuxun: A popular hit until Mao wrote an editorial condemning it, launching the first film purge of the new republic.
f:xala: A businessman is struck impotent on the night he takes a third wife; a satire of Senegal’s new elite.
f:xmen: Its lead replaced another actor three weeks into shooting; launched the modern superhero cycle.
f:yassinarmy: Part of a hugely popular comedy series that sent its star into every branch of the forces.
f:yellowcocoon: After his sister-in-law dies, a man carries her body back to their home village and searches for his missing brother. Three hours of long, drifting takes; its director’s first feature.
f:yellowearth: A soldier collects folk songs on the Loess Plateau; the first Fifth Generation film to reach the West.
f:yentl83: She spent fifteen years getting it made and was the first woman to write, produce, direct and star in a studio film.
f:yiyi: Its director’s last film; never released in Taiwan in his lifetime.
f:yojimbo: A ronin plays two gangs against each other; remade without permission as an Italian western that started a craze.
f:yol: Written in prison by its director, who sent orders to a stand-in; he escaped Turkey to edit it. Banned there until 1999.
f:yolo24: Its director and star lost about 50 kilograms over the shoot, playing a woman who takes up boxing.
f:youcancount: A playwright’s first film, about a single mother whose drifting brother comes home; made its supporting actor.
f:youngfrankenstein: Shot in black-and-white using the original 1931 laboratory props, found in a storeroom.
f:yourname: A Tokyo boy and a country girl swap bodies; the highest-grossing anime not by Miyazaki, at the time.
f:ytumama: Two teenagers and an older woman on a road trip; a narrator steps in with what the characters don’t know about Mexico around them.
f:zanjeer: Created its lead’s "angry young man" and made him a star after a dozen flops.
f:zatoichi: The first adventure of a blind masseur swordsman; 26 films followed.
f:zerodeconduite: A boarding-school revolt, banned in France until after the war.
f:zhivago: Russia recreated in Spain, including a Moscow street built near Madrid; reviews were poor and audiences flocked.
f:zmovie: A thinly veiled account of a Greek politician’s murder; the junta banned it, and the Greek letter for "he lives" became a slogan.
f:zoneofinterest: The Auschwitz commandant’s family lives an ordinary life beside the camp wall; the horror is only heard. Hidden cameras around the house ran with no crew in the rooms.
f:zootopia2: Earned more in China than at home, and became the highest-grossing Hollywood animated film.
f:zorro: The first swashbuckler, which turned a comedy star into an action hero.
p:aalberg: RKO’s sound director, who mixed a newspaper tycoon’s echoing mansion.
p:aamir: Made one film a year at most, and pasted his own debut’s posters on rickshaws himself.
p:abbasi_a: An Iranian-born director working out of Denmark whose Border won Un Certain Regard at Cannes.
p:abbott_lb: Sank an ocean liner and burned a skyscraper for the master of disaster.
p:abdelsalam: A production designer for foreign epics who directed one feature, about tomb robbers, and spent the rest of his life on a second.
p:abdi: Earned an Oscar nomination for his very first screen role, opposite Tom Hanks.
p:abraham_y: An Israeli journalist who co-directed the Oscar-winning No Other Land with Palestinian activist Basel Adra.
p:abrams: A TV creator who rebooted a starship with lens flares.
p:acharya_vk: Wrote all three Dhoom films before directing the third.
p:ackroyd: Ken Loach’s cameraman, who shot a bomb squad in Jordan with four handheld cameras.
p:adam_k: A Berlin refugee and RAF pilot who designed a war room with a round table and a volcano lair.
p:adams_a: Nominated for six acting Oscars without a win.
p:addison: Wrote the harpsichord romp for a bawdy period comedy.
p:adelove: A travelling-theatre star whose films played in the open air across Yorubaland.
p:adilbilall: A Belgian-Moroccan duo whose finished Batgirl was shelved by Warner Bros.
p:adoor: Founded a film co-operative in Kerala and made a film every few years, each one slow and exact.
p:adra: A Palestinian activist from Masafer Yatta who filmed his own village’s demolitions for No Other Land.
